0.long_answer: Hurler syndrome, also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I), is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme alpha-L-iduronidase. This enzyme is responsible for breaking down glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) such as dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate. When alpha-L-iduronidase is deficient, these complex sugars accumulate in the lysosomes of cells, leading to progressive cellular and tissue damage. The buildup of GAGs results in the clinical manifestations of Hurler syndrome, which include developmental delays, coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, and cardiopulmonary complications, ultimately affecting multiple organ systems.

1.long_answer: The enzyme iduronidase, which normally hydrolyzes the α-L-iduronic acid residues of dermatan sulfate and heparin sulfate, is deficient in patients with MPS I disorders such as Hurler syndrome. The commercialized variant of this enzyme, produced using recombinant DNA technology in Chinese hamster ovaries, is known as Aldurazyme. This enzyme replacement therapy is used to treat individuals affected by different forms of MPS I, including Hurler, Hurler-Scheie, and Scheie syndromes.
